The rankings of universities fluctuate every year and there is very little difference between the top universities. The rankings which I think you are referring to (QS) are notorious for not being particularly reliable.

Now, to answer your question;

Imperial College is just a science specialist university whereas Oxford offers all types of subjects (quite strong in it's humanities departments). So we can only compare the Science and Engineering departments.

Even limiting the discussion to just the science/engineering departments of the 2 universities, different departments within the university tend to be better/worse. Since I have some knowledge of the computing departments of the 2 universities I will try to compare them:

1. Prestige: Both the universities are very well respected for computing. In the UK, both the universities have an equally strong reputation. Outside of the UK, Oxford being an older university will be more recognised by the layman (although Imperial is quickly making it's name known, so this advantage may disappear in a few years). Also Oxford is renowned for providing tutorials with professors in small group sessions , but Imperial College also provides a personal programming and maths tutor, so I think they are both equal in this aspect. Another point is that the number of students studying Computer Science at Oxford is smaller than that at Imperial, thus providing a stronger community feel. So I would say that Oxford has the advantage here.   
Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 0

2. Entry Requirements:

I can confidently say that Imperial wins in this aspect. From first hand experience:  
Most offer holders this year for oxford got an offer of A*AAA (with the A* in maths) without any additional requirements whereas for Imperial College most of the offers given out were A*A*AA(with A*'s in maths and further maths) + STEP* papers (+EPQ* in some cases). Imperial has another course called Joint Maths and Computing in which the offers were even higher! Students had to sit the STEP III*exam, a VERY rigorous and tough exam( the hardest of the STEP papers).

Also, in the UK (for computing /engineering) it is a general trend that the best students apply to Cambridge which means that they can't apply to Oxford, but they can still apply to Imperial College. So these students end up choosing between Cambridge and Imperial College; although most choose Cambridge, a significant proportion end up at Imperial.

Also, I don't know why but many intelligent international students tend to choose Imperial College. These factors mean that Oxford may lose out on the best minds.

Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 1

3. Course Content and Job prospects

Imperial College has the advantage of location; being in London, students have access to the best companies and banks at their doorstep and the university is very well connected with industry. In fact, if you're on the 4 year course, in your last year you have to do do a 6 month internship. I found out on TSR* that there are many more job offers than students available, and the students end up with quite a few job offers from top companies (Google, Facebook, Goldman Sachs, etc.). At the Imperial College interview, one of the professors told me that Morgan Stanley (one of the top investment banks) first recruits students of Imperial College and only then looks elsewhere. He told me that the companies often complain why they don't have more students. He even said that one of the companies remarked that Imperial College students are even better than MIT students! (I would take that with a pinch of salt though).

I'm sure Oxford also provides the students fantastic job opportunities, but the course is more theoretical and less focused on industry. Also, Oxford being a small town(although some people prefer this), just can't match up with London.

Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 2

Conclusion: First of all a reasonable comparison of the 2 universities can only be made for specific science departments. Within the Engineering/Computing domain, Imperial's reputation is stellar. Yes, Imperial College is better than Oxford (and this shouldn't be extremely surprising!) but not because of the reason you said (that it is higher ranked). The actual reasons for this are mentioned above.

Perhaps a better question would be to compare Cambridge and Imperial College for computing ;)!

* STEP: A maths admission test used by Cambridhe university for entrance to Maths courses. They are considered to be very hard and require a lot of mathematical maturity and perseverance). There are 3 step papers, STEP I, STEP II, STEP III

EPQ : Extended Project Qualification. It is taken by some students in Britain if they wish to research into some topic.

TSR: A British website for university admissions. I highly recommend it if you are planning on applying to British universities.

“AHAHAAHAHAHAHA IN YOUR FACE CAMBRIDGE AHAHAHAHAAHAHAH”

Ahem.

Let me start that again.

What I mean to say is this:

I don’t really find it relevant. I don’t find university comparisons that useful. I mean - which part of the university are they comparing?

Are they comparing:

*   Undergraduate
*   Postgraduate
*   Postdoctoral research
*   Individual subjects
*   Student satisfaction

Because all of things vary wildly across a university - a university could have a fantastic undergraduate scheme in economics - which drags them up the ratings, but that doesn’t tell me anything about postgraduate chemistry. For example, Imperial is nominally slightly better than Oxford at physics….but that isn’t reflected in these rankings, so how does this ranking help a physics applicant?

You need to make sure you are comparing like-for-like, and to my mind, such overarching league tables fail to do this.

This is complicated even further by the fact that the instituion Oxford pipped to the post (CalTech) is an American university, which uses the American Major/Minor/StudyWhatYouLikeUntilYouPickAMajor system - whereas at Oxford we us the UK system, whereby you apply to study a specific subject, and then study only that subject (although Cambridge offers something similar in the natural sciences).

So if you’re an undergraduate trying to decide to apply to a UK or a US university, this comparison isn’t at all helpful - it is placing two utterly different systems in a direct comparison, which is misleading at best.

Much more useful rankings are those which take into account

*   The subject you want to study (if you are looking at physics, only look at the physics rankings for crying out loud - you don’t care that Oxford is great at PPE!)
*   The country you are applying for
*   The level at which you are interested in (Imperial is notorious for having a great postgrad focus, but neglecting its undergrads…so as an undergrad you don’t want to know about how great postgrad is!)

So in summary, such sweeping comparisons are not really useful. I really hope no-one is basing application decisions off them (who am I kidding, of course they are!), much more useful are the narrowed-down rankings.

All of this is ignoring the fact that the top few universities are so close together as to make no difference. Oxford and Cambridge regularly swap places in the UK rankings - and Imperial and Durham are so close behind as to be pretty much negligible.

Rankings don’t really matter, people.

But, still:

Sort of depends what you mean by “at the top”. But if you mean “in the best 1%” then probably for a long while yet. Let’s look at the history of global universities.

*   1,000 years ago. The first universities start. The first (and best) universities in the world are all located in Northern Italy - home the most powerful Duchies in the world.
*   500 years ago. First universities in the New World are founded by Spain in Latin America. But these universities fail to develop into global elites.
*   400 years ago. The enlightenment. Oxford and Cambridge, fuelled by scholars from the continent begin to challenge their global hegemony.
*   200 years ago. Industrial revolution. UK becomes world’s pre-eminent power. Oxbridge become the world’s pre-eminent universities.
*   100 years ago. America becomes world’s pre-eminent power. People begin to suspect that the best American universities are at least peers to Oxford and Cambridge. New schools like MIT and Stanford focus on new and developing STEM fields.
*   50 years ago. American universities begin to be recognised as dominant globally.

Which takes us up to about now. Oxford is certainly still amongst the world’s very best, although there are plenty who claim (with good reason) it has been surpassed by many of America’s best universities.

What will happen in the future? I suspect in the near term America’s universities will pull further ahead. They have an excellent product, a global reputation, and are extremely well funded. Moreover the “money gap” is only going to get wider. Leading American private universities charge around $60,000 a year, and people are queueing up to pay. Those billion dollar endowments won’t shrink any time soon. Oxford charges £9,250 a year and people bitch and moan about it constantly. (With some justification - most European universities are free.)

Further down the line? China and India are rising as global powers. If our timeline above is any guide, their academic institutions will see their global standing rise commensurately - one day we may see Tsinghua and IITB challenging Harvard and MIT. At the moment academic fraud is rife in those countries which damages the reputation of their flagship universities. But it is unlikely to remain that way forever.

A university is comprised of too many separate parts to be judged as a whole unit - and different universities have different systems (the UK/US divide is a particular point of contention).

What might be the best for one person, is not necessarily the best for another person.

So whilst Oxford did score highest on the THE rankings, I dispute that it is the “best” university because I don’t believe that there is a single “best” university.

There is only the best university for you.

I’m grateful to [Jack Fraser-Govil](https://www.quora.com/profile/Jack-Fraser-Govil "www.quora.com") for drawing my attention to this question.

The Times Higher Education World University Rankings are a massive, bloated exercise in marketing, self-importance and vanity. Ironically for a newspaper that is focussed on “the academy”, its analysis is statistically worthless.

Jack has offered a solid rebuttal, but I’d like to add a point or two of my own.

Suppose you are six foot tall and I am five foot tall. Then you are 20% taller than I am. Suppose you are 25 years old and I am 50 years old. Then I am twice as old as you are.

How happy are you today? Five? I’m eight. Who’s happier? Me? How much happier? 60%?

Feet and years are well-behaved units. Their scales are what we call interval-ratio scales. Dividing numbers in these scales has a meaningful interpretation.

Happiness does not have well-defined units, let alone well-behaved ones. It’s perfectly possible that my eight makes me less happy than your five. If that even means anything. You don’t know (and can’t know) my scale and vice versa.

Who’s the best looking character in Game of Thrones? Well, at least we can all agree on that. Jon Snow, right? Wrong, it’s Theon Greyjoy.

Beauty doesn’t have well-defined units, either.

So exactly what is the THE ranking? They’ll tell you their methodology. And it’s (a) completely arbitrary (b) includes elements that have no well-defined scale of measurement and (c) combines these arbitrary, not-all-well-defined scores in an arbitrary way. You could change any element and get a different ranking.

No ranking system for universities will be meaningful because you cannot compare vast, disparate, institutions, except in trivial ways. Harvard probably has more money than any other university. You can say that. (And money is a well-behaved unit. Except it’s not because there are lots of units for money and they all mean different things and they cannot easily be compared. See The Economist’s ‘Big Mac index’ for an attempt to do so. Even that fails. You can’t buy a Big Mac in India.)

But so what if Harvard has lots of money? What useful information does that give, say, a prospective student?

I enjoy reminding Jack Fraser that one college at Cambridge has on its own won more Nobel prizes in Physics than the entire university of Oxford. This claim is wholly spurious because universities don’t win Nobel prizes, people do. And associating people with specific universities often involves a certain degree of creativity. (Cambridge likes to boast of Newton and Darwin, neither of whom did their celebrated work at the university itself.)

The point of the THE WUR is that it makes the publishers of the THE and the people who work for it feel important. Its publication attracts global attention and that boosts sales of the magazine and advertising revenue. The staff who work on the WUR get to travel the world. They host lavish dinners. It’s all very exciting.

And utterly meaningless.

[What do you think of Oxford coming top of the 2016 Times Higher Education (THE) rankings?](https://www.quora.com/What-do-you-think-of-Oxford-coming-top-of-the-2016-Times-Higher-Education-THE-rankings/answer/Jack-Fraser-Govil "www.quora.com")

Whilst of course, the sentiment of me wetting myself laughing at beating Cambridge still stands, I will focus on the more serious parts.

As far as I can see, there are a few major problems with these kind of global comparisons, and they are:

* * *

Different university systems

All UK universities follow roughly the same format for undergraduate (pick a subject before, study only that), and all US universities follow roughly the same format (a major/minor system) — but these systems are bloody difficult to compare.

The UK goes for a depth-first approach to university education at the expense of breadth, whilst the US goes for a breadth first approach at the expense of depth.

That means that I will come out of university having done far more physics than a physics major — but said physics major will also have studied history, or literature, and hence have a wider knowledge base than me.

How do you compare universities which take two such different approaches to teaching students?

If a ranking system such as [QS World University Rankings](https://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2018 "www.topuniversities.com")tells me that MIT and CalTech are better than Oxford — Oxford is still better for me, because I prefer the UK approach.

Some people will prefer the US approach — and that’s absolutely fine — Oxford isn’t the best university for those people.

The problem is there’s no indication on either the THE or QS lists about the wildly different approaches each of these universities take — and yet they still find a way to rank them on the same scale?

Seems barmy to me.

* * *

Global Comparison of a Large Institution

This type of ranking assigns an entire university a score and ranks them accordingly — but the ranking doesn’t actually tell you anything useful, because a university is composed of several parts.

You’ve got the undergraduates, postgraduates and researchers — and each of those is split up into subject-based departments.

They then take an average (or some other way of collating scores) across all of these disparate entities, and call that the univerisity’s score.

But…that doesn’t help.

A student doesn’t attend an mushed together average of undergraduate-postgraduate-researcher positions over an average of all subjects, do they? They attend a set course, and take a finite number of courses.

When I was applying to Oxford, I couldn’t really care less if Oxford was great for postgraduate research into music theory — what I cared about was undergraduate physics.

So what purpose does collating all these unrelated components of a university have? It certainly doesn’t help inform students — because they are (or at least should be) only interested in how the university ranks in the bits that are relevant to them — and these lists do not have that information in them — in my case, this list tells me absolutely nothing about undergraduate physics.

* * *

Rapid Switching of University Places

This year, the THE top 10 is as follows:

1.   Oxford
2.   Cambridge
3.   Caltech == Stanford
4.   []
5.   MIT
6.   Harvard
7.   Princeton
8.   Imperial College, London
9.   Chicago
10.   Pennsylvania == ETH Zurich

Last year, the list was:

1.   Oxford
2.   Caltech
3.   Stanford
4.   Cambridge
5.   MIT
6.   Harvard
7.   Prinecton
8.   Imperial College
9.   ETH Zurich
10.   Berkeley == Chicago

So. Do you really believe that in a single year, that much can change?

This year, Berkeley is at 18th. Berkeley dropped 8 places. In 12 months!

These institutions do not change that rapidly.

It’s insane to suggest that anything at Cambridge, CalTech or Stanford has changed so dramatically as to alter their positions like that — and Berkeley hasn’t suddenly become a worse place to learn in the last year.

The scale of these rapid changes (and also the fact that different ranking systems rank the same set of universities differently) is that the ranking systems are changing faster than the universities.

Do you really think anyone would care about the THE rankings, if they were the same 10 universities, in the same order year, on year?

Sure, over a decade or so, there would be changes — but on a year-on-year basis?

That’s ridiculous!

All that’s happening is that the ranking people are ranking different things with different weights this year, or their research methodology changes slightly.

* * *

In conclusion, I just don’t think these types of rankings are particularly useful — there’s too many variables, the rankings change far quicker than the institutions possibly can, and I just cannot see the point of such a global comparison.

Who do these rankings help? All they do is give prospective students the wrong ideas about where and why they should apply to go to university.

That being said:

Hahahahahahahahahahahahahahahhahaha suck on that Cambridge! TWO YEARS IN A ROW, HAHAHAHAHAHAHAAHAAHAHAHAHAHA.

The Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings 2018 placed the University of Oxford at number one, continuing its position at the top of that particular annual list. Whether this “consolidates its position as the best university in the world” depends on how one interprets “best” and which evidence one weighs.

Key facts

*   THE 2018: Oxford ranked 1st. Cambridge was 2nd; Stanford, MIT and Harvard followed among the top five.
*   Oxford had previously taken the THE top spot in 2016 and 2017 (THE introduced its current methodology in 2010; Oxford has frequently appeared at or near the top in recent years).
*   Different global rankings use different methodologies (THE, QS, ARWU/Shanghai, US News, etc.), and they do not always agree. For example, QS and ARWU have alternated other institutions (e.g., MIT, Stanford, Harvard) at the top in various years.

Why rankings differ

*   Methodology: THE weights teaching, research, citations, international outlook and industry income. Other rankings emphasize employer reputation, faculty/student ratios, research output, or Nobel/Field prizes.
*   Indicator sensitivity: Small changes in citation counts, survey responses or research income can shift places near the top because scores are tightly clustered.
*   Time horizon: Some rankings reward long-term historical achievements (prizes, alumni), others emphasize recent research influence (citations).

What “consolidated” would reasonably mean

*   Repeated top placement across multiple independent, reputable rankings over several years would constitute consolidation.
*   THE alone giving Oxford first place in 2018 is strong evidence of excellence but not definitive proof that Oxford is unambiguously the world’s best by all reasonable measures.

Practical interpretation

*   Oxford’s 2018 THE #1 confirms its standing among a small group of elite, top-tier global research universities.
*   Claims that it has “consolidated” an uncontested position as the single best university are overstated if based only on THE 2018; a more measured conclusion is that Oxford reinforced its place at the very top of global rankings in 2018, alongside peers like MIT, Stanford, Harvard and Cambridge.

Contextual note

*   Rankings are one useful, imperfect tool for assessing universities; decisions about “best” should consider specific disciplines, teaching quality, resources, fit for student needs and research strengths as well as multiple ranking systems.

Global Problems — Hope for a More United Humanity

As civilization develops, humanity faces problems of ever greater scale, affecting not just individual countries but the world as a whole. Climate change, the threat of major wars, the loss of biodiversity, the depletion of natural resources, shortages of fresh water, new pandemics, mass migrations, the rapid development of artificial intelligence, and many other challenges all demand ever closer international cooperation. For all their diversity, they share one important feature: no single country is capable of solving these problems entirely on its own.

A natural question arises: can global problems become not only a source of new dangers, but also one of the forces shaping the further evolution of human civilization?

To understand this better, it is enough to consider one of the most serious challenges of our time — climate change.

Climate change is no longer a hypothesis, but one of the most reliably predicted global processes of the twenty-first century. Its consequences affect virtually every country: rising global sea levels, the melting of glaciers, the growing frequency of extreme weather events, droughts, floods, and forest fires, the shrinking of fresh-water reserves, the worsening of conditions for agriculture, the loss of biodiversity, the rise of climate migration, and vast economic losses.

History shows that in the face of a common threat, people and states often begin to cooperate more closely. When a problem cannot be solved alone, cooperation ceases to be a matter of political idealism and becomes a vital necessity.

Does climate change guarantee that all countries will draw closer together? Of course not. Common threats can not only bring countries together, but also intensify competition for resources, political disagreements, and migration crises. Yet history also reveals another pattern: the greater the scale of shared problems, the stronger the need for international coordination becomes.

This is precisely why climate change may well become one of the catalysts for closer international cooperation and help bring states closer together.

This is where hope emerges. Not the hope that global problems will disappear, but the hope that they will help humanity grasp a simple truth more quickly: in a world where ever more threats are becoming common to all, the long-term well-being of every nation increasingly depends on cooperation among all nations.

Perhaps humanity’s greatest hope lies in this: that it is precisely our shared challenges that will gradually teach us to see one another not as rivals, but as participants in a common destiny. If this historical pattern holds, then one of the manifestations of the further evolution of human civilization may be humanity’s gradual movement toward greater unity.

The rankings of universities fluctuate every year and there is very little difference between the top universities. The rankings which I think you are referring to (QS) are notorious for not being particularly reliable.

Now, to answer your question;

Imperial College is just a science specialist university whereas Oxford offers all types of subjects (quite strong in it's humanities departments). So we can only compare the Science and Engineering departments.

Even limiting the discussion to just the science/engineering departments of the 2 universities, different departments within the university tend to be better/worse. Since I have some knowledge of the computing departments of the 2 universities I will try to compare them:

1. Prestige: Both the universities are very well respected for computing. In the UK, both the universities have an equally strong reputation. Outside of the UK, Oxford being an older university will be more recognised by the layman (although Imperial is quickly making it's name known, so this advantage may disappear in a few years). Also Oxford is renowned for providing tutorials with professors in small group sessions , but Imperial College also provides a personal programming and maths tutor, so I think they are both equal in this aspect. Another point is that the number of students studying Computer Science at Oxford is smaller than that at Imperial, thus providing a stronger community feel. So I would say that Oxford has the advantage here.   
Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 0

2. Entry Requirements:

I can confidently say that Imperial wins in this aspect. From first hand experience:  
Most offer holders this year for oxford got an offer of A*AAA (with the A* in maths) without any additional requirements whereas for Imperial College most of the offers given out were A*A*AA(with A*'s in maths and further maths) + STEP* papers (+EPQ* in some cases). Imperial has another course called Joint Maths and Computing in which the offers were even higher! Students had to sit the STEP III*exam, a VERY rigorous and tough exam( the hardest of the STEP papers).

Also, in the UK (for computing /engineering) it is a general trend that the best students apply to Cambridge which means that they can't apply to Oxford, but they can still apply to Imperial College. So these students end up choosing between Cambridge and Imperial College; although most choose Cambridge, a significant proportion end up at Imperial.

Also, I don't know why but many intelligent international students tend to choose Imperial College. These factors mean that Oxford may lose out on the best minds.

Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 1

3. Course Content and Job prospects

Imperial College has the advantage of location; being in London, students have access to the best companies and banks at their doorstep and the university is very well connected with industry. In fact, if you're on the 4 year course, in your last year you have to do do a 6 month internship. I found out on TSR* that there are many more job offers than students available, and the students end up with quite a few job offers from top companies (Google, Facebook, Goldman Sachs, etc.). At the Imperial College interview, one of the professors told me that Morgan Stanley (one of the top investment banks) first recruits students of Imperial College and only then looks elsewhere. He told me that the companies often complain why they don't have more students. He even said that one of the companies remarked that Imperial College students are even better than MIT students! (I would take that with a pinch of salt though).

I'm sure Oxford also provides the students fantastic job opportunities, but the course is more theoretical and less focused on industry. Also, Oxford being a small town(although some people prefer this), just can't match up with London.

Oxford : 1 , Imperial: 2

Conclusion: First of all a reasonable comparison of the 2 universities can only be made for specific science departments. Within the Engineering/Computing domain, Imperial's reputation is stellar. Yes, Imperial College is better than Oxford (and this shouldn't be extremely surprising!) but not because of the reason you said (that it is higher ranked). The actual reasons for this are mentioned above.

Perhaps a better question would be to compare Cambridge and Imperial College for computing ;)!

Because all of things vary wildly across a university - a university could have a fantastic undergraduate scheme in economics - which drags them up the ratings, but that doesn’t tell me anything about postgraduate chemistry. For example, Imperial is nominally slightly better than Oxford at physics….but that isn’t reflected in these rankings, so how does this ranking help a physics applicant?

You need to make sure you are comparing like-for-like, and to my mind, such overarching league tables fail to do this.

This is complicated even further by the fact that the instituion Oxford pipped to the post (CalTech) is an American university, which uses the American Major/Minor/StudyWhatYouLikeUntilYouPickAMajor system - whereas at Oxford we us the UK system, whereby you apply to study a specific subject, and then study only that subject (although Cambridge offers something similar in the natural sciences).

So if you’re an undergraduate trying to decide to apply to a UK or a US university, this comparison isn’t at all helpful - it is placing two utterly different systems in a direct comparison, which is misleading at best.

Much more useful rankings are those which take into account

*   The subject you want to study (if you are looking at physics, only look at the physics rankings for crying out loud - you don’t care that Oxford is great at PPE!)
*   The country you are applying for
*   The level at which you are interested in (Imperial is notorious for having a great postgrad focus, but neglecting its undergrads…so as an undergrad you don’t want to know about how great postgrad is!)

So in summary, such sweeping comparisons are not really useful. I really hope no-one is basing application decisions off them (who am I kidding, of course they are!), much more useful are the narrowed-down rankings.

All of this is ignoring the fact that the top few universities are so close together as to make no difference. Oxford and Cambridge regularly swap places in the UK rankings - and Imperial and Durham are so close behind as to be pretty much negligible.

Rankings don’t really matter, people.

Sort of depends what you mean by “at the top”. But if you mean “in the best 1%” then probably for a long while yet. Let’s look at the history of global universities.

*   1,000 years ago. The first universities start. The first (and best) universities in the world are all located in Northern Italy - home the most powerful Duchies in the world.
*   500 years ago. First universities in the New World are founded by Spain in Latin America. But these universities fail to develop into global elites.
*   400 years ago. The enlightenment. Oxford and Cambridge, fuelled by scholars from the continent begin to challenge their global hegemony.
*   200 years ago. Industrial revolution. UK becomes world’s pre-eminent power. Oxbridge become the world’s pre-eminent universities.
*   100 years ago. America becomes world’s pre-eminent power. People begin to suspect that the best American universities are at least peers to Oxford and Cambridge. New schools like MIT and Stanford focus on new and developing STEM fields.
*   50 years ago. American universities begin to be recognised as dominant globally.

Which takes us up to about now. Oxford is certainly still amongst the world’s very best, although there are plenty who claim (with good reason) it has been surpassed by many of America’s best universities.

What will happen in the future? I suspect in the near term America’s universities will pull further ahead. They have an excellent product, a global reputation, and are extremely well funded. Moreover the “money gap” is only going to get wider. Leading American private universities charge around $60,000 a year, and people are queueing up to pay. Those billion dollar endowments won’t shrink any time soon. Oxford charges £9,250 a year and people bitch and moan about it constantly. (With some justification - most European universities are free.)

Further down the line? China and India are rising as global powers. If our timeline above is any guide, their academic institutions will see their global standing rise commensurately - one day we may see Tsinghua and IITB challenging Harvard and MIT. At the moment academic fraud is rife in those countries which damages the reputation of their flagship universities. But it is unlikely to remain that way forever.

Well, no. It means “by the criteria selected by the Times Higher Education people, and using their specific weighting, Oxford is the highest scoring university”.

That’s not the same as best - because “best” is highly subjective. If you wanted to study Marine Biology, for example - Oxford isn’t very good. It’s quite far from the sea, for one thing!

I’ve written about how I dislike these wide ranging league tables earlier today ([Jack Fraser-Govil's answer to What do you think of Oxford coming top of the 2016 Times Higher Education (THE) rankings?](https://www.quora.com/What-do-you-think-of-Oxford-coming-top-of-the-2016-Times-Higher-Education-THE-rankings/answer/Jack-Fraser-Govil "www.quora.com")) and if you read that, you will understand that a global “score” for a university doesn’t really make sense to me.

A university is comprised of too many separate parts to be judged as a whole unit - and different universities have different systems (the UK/US divide is a particular point of contention).

What might be the best for one person, is not necessarily the best for another person.

So whilst Oxford did score highest on the THE rankings, I dispute that it is the “best” university because I don’t believe that there is a single “best” university.

There is only the best university for you.

And as long as you’re happy knowing that your university was the best for you? Well anyone saying otherwise can go fuck themselves, as far as I’m concerned ;p

![Image 5: Daytime panorama of Oxford with the Radcliffe Camera to the foreground](https://www.alumni.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_large/public/alumni/images/media/radcliffe-camera-aerial.jpeg?itok=IpUvi7On)

## OXFORD RETAINS FIRST PLACE IN WORLD UNIVERSITY RANKINGS

**Oxford University has topped the THE World University Rankings for a fifth consecutive year**

Published: 17 September 2020

**Share this article**

[Share on facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)[Share on twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)[Share via email](mailto:?&subject=Check%20out%20this%20page%20I%20found%20on%20Oxford%20Alumni&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)

Oxford University’s enduring global reputation, cutting edge research and unique teaching environment have helped the University retain first place in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings for a fifth year in a row.

The announcement was made on Wednesday 2 September as this year’s international rankings were unveiled at the THE’s World Academic Summit.

The Vice-Chancellor of Oxford University, Professor Louise Richardson, said: ‘We are delighted to have consolidated our position at the top of the THE World University Rankings this year.

‘The international standing of British Higher Education is a testament to generations of investment in education as well as to our extraordinarily talented staff and students.

‘The COVID-19 pandemic, which has posed such a threat to higher education around the world, has also demonstrated the critical role universities play in addressing global challenges.’

Phil Baty, Chief Knowledge Officer at the Times Higher Education, said the result was testament to Oxford excelling across all indicators assessed by the rankings. He added that the University’s international outlook had been a particular point of excellence.

He explained: ‘The Times Higher Education World University Rankings deploy a comprehensive and balanced range of 13 separate performance indicators to cover world-class research universities’ core missions, across teaching, research, knowledge transfer and international outlook.

‘Under the current decade-old methodology, no university has ever topped the THE World University Rankings for five consecutive annual editions.

‘So this year’s rankings results are a testament not only to Oxford’s enduring reputation among leading scholars globally, but also to its ability to continually innovate, publishing cutting edge research with the highest global impact across a wide range of disciplines and providing a uniquely stimulating teaching environment.

‘Oxford excels across all of our indicators, but its international outlook scores in particular stand out against world top-ten peers in the US. That commitment to international collaboration and partnership, should be cherished and protected.’

The award follows a year when the University of Oxford has been at the centre of international attention for its work on finding a[vaccine for COVID-19](https://www.research.ox.ac.uk/Area/coronavirus-research/vaccine)as well as taking a leading role in trialling therapeutic drugs and antibody testing. The University has also been working on a wide range of projects including the development of mental health interventions for NHS staff experiencing trauma, research into the impacts of the crisis on parents and practical resources for families, novel virus detection methods, as well as analysis of the actions taken by governments across the world as they respond to the pandemic.

In June this year the University also announced a landmark[£80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2020-06-11-reuben-foundation-donates-80-million-first-new-oxford-college-30-years)– one of the largest in its history – to support Oxford’s newest graduate college. The new college in the heart of the University’s science area will focus on interdisciplinary research addressing future global challenges. The gift will also fund a major new graduate scholarship programme. The college – the University’s 39th and its first for 30 years – will be named Reuben College in recognition of the historic gift, and is due to welcome its first students in the autumn of 2021.

[View the full THE World University Rankings 2021 here](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2021/world-ranking)

# OXFORD RETAINS FIRST PLACE IN WORLD UNIVERSITY RANKINGS

![Image 5: Daytime panorama of Oxford with the Radcliffe Camera to the foreground](https://www.alumni.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/styles/mt_image_large/public/alumni/images/media/radcliffe-camera-aerial.jpeg?itok=IpUvi7On)

## OXFORD RETAINS FIRST PLACE IN WORLD UNIVERSITY RANKINGS

**Oxford University has topped the THE World University Rankings for a fifth consecutive year**

Published: 17 September 2020

**Share this article**

[Share on facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)[Share on twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)[Share via email](mailto:?&subject=Check%20out%20this%20page%20I%20found%20on%20Oxford%20Alumni&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.alumni.ox.ac.uk%2Farticle%2Foxford-retains-first-place-in-world-university-rankings)

Oxford University’s enduring global reputation, cutting edge research and unique teaching environment have helped the University retain first place in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings for a fifth year in a row.

The announcement was made on Wednesday 2 September as this year’s international rankings were unveiled at the THE’s World Academic Summit.

The Vice-Chancellor of Oxford University, Professor Louise Richardson, said: ‘We are delighted to have consolidated our position at the top of the THE World University Rankings this year.

‘The international standing of British Higher Education is a testament to generations of investment in education as well as to our extraordinarily talented staff and students.

‘The COVID-19 pandemic, which has posed such a threat to higher education around the world, has also demonstrated the critical role universities play in addressing global challenges.’

Phil Baty, Chief Knowledge Officer at the Times Higher Education, said the result was testament to Oxford excelling across all indicators assessed by the rankings. He added that the University’s international outlook had been a particular point of excellence.

He explained: ‘The Times Higher Education World University Rankings deploy a comprehensive and balanced range of 13 separate performance indicators to cover world-class research universities’ core missions, across teaching, research, knowledge transfer and international outlook.

‘Under the current decade-old methodology, no university has ever topped the THE World University Rankings for five consecutive annual editions.

‘So this year’s rankings results are a testament not only to Oxford’s enduring reputation among leading scholars globally, but also to its ability to continually innovate, publishing cutting edge research with the highest global impact across a wide range of disciplines and providing a uniquely stimulating teaching environment.

‘Oxford excels across all of our indicators, but its international outlook scores in particular stand out against world top-ten peers in the US. That commitment to international collaboration and partnership, should be cherished and protected.’

The award follows a year when the University of Oxford has been at the centre of international attention for its work on finding a[vaccine for COVID-19](https://www.research.ox.ac.uk/Area/coronavirus-research/vaccine)as well as taking a leading role in trialling therapeutic drugs and antibody testing. The University has also been working on a wide range of projects including the development of mental health interventions for NHS staff experiencing trauma, research into the impacts of the crisis on parents and practical resources for families, novel virus detection methods, as well as analysis of the actions taken by governments across the world as they respond to the pandemic.

In June this year the University also announced a landmark[£80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation](https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2020-06-11-reuben-foundation-donates-80-million-first-new-oxford-college-30-years)– one of the largest in its history – to support Oxford’s newest graduate college. The new college in the heart of the University’s science area will focus on interdisciplinary research addressing future global challenges. The gift will also fund a major new graduate scholarship programme. The college – the University’s 39th and its first for 30 years – will be named Reuben College in recognition of the historic gift, and is due to welcome its first students in the autumn of 2021.

[View the full THE World University Rankings 2021 here](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2021/world-ranking)

# University of Oxford Tops Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2018

Check out the list.

By [Rachel Jacoby Zoldan](https://www.teenvogue.com/contributor/rachel-jacoby-zoldan)

September 5, 2017

It seems that every day there's a new college ranking system, whether it be the school with the best [value](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/forbes-ranks-best-value-colleges) — or the [most parties](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/princeton-review-2018-college-rankings). But the best universities in the world have been compiled for 2018 in one neat list from the [_Times Higher Education_](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) and its corresponding, in-depth [data report](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2018/world-ranking#!/page/0/length/25/locations/CA/sort_by/rank/sort_order/asc/cols/stats). And for the first time _ever_, the U.K. snagged the top two spots, with Oxford University coming in at number one and Cambridge University just behind it at number two.

To definitively rank the universities, of which they culled data from thousands of in over 77 countries, the _Times Higher Education_[looked at five primary factors](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/methodology-world-university-rankings-2018) within each school: "research, teaching, research influence, industry income, and international outlook." Translation: They looked at each college or university's learning environment, the overall efficacy and success of its research, and generally how well knowledge flows on campus. Oxford University was the overall best for the second year in a row; it's the oldest university in the U.K. and an approximate 95% of students post-graduation find employment within six months.

But it wasn't just the Brits at the top — the U.S. took the remaining eight spots to round out the top 10 universities. Other countries in the "best of" conversation include Canada, China, and Switzerland. Check out the 10 best universities (OK, 12, since there were two ties) in the world below, then head over to _Times Higher Education_ to see [the full list](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) — and where your school nets out. You might just find something to inspire you to take action and foster change.

# University of Oxford Tops Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2018

Check out the list.

By [Rachel Jacoby Zoldan](https://www.teenvogue.com/contributor/rachel-jacoby-zoldan)

September 5, 2017

It seems that every day there's a new college ranking system, whether it be the school with the best [value](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/forbes-ranks-best-value-colleges) — or the [most parties](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/princeton-review-2018-college-rankings). But the best universities in the world have been compiled for 2018 in one neat list from the [_Times Higher Education_](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) and its corresponding, in-depth [data report](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2018/world-ranking#!/page/0/length/25/locations/CA/sort_by/rank/sort_order/asc/cols/stats). And for the first time _ever_, the U.K. snagged the top two spots, with Oxford University coming in at number one and Cambridge University just behind it at number two.

To definitively rank the universities, of which they culled data from thousands of in over 77 countries, the _Times Higher Education_[looked at five primary factors](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/methodology-world-university-rankings-2018) within each school: "research, teaching, research influence, industry income, and international outlook." Translation: They looked at each college or university's learning environment, the overall efficacy and success of its research, and generally how well knowledge flows on campus. Oxford University was the overall best for the second year in a row; it's the oldest university in the U.K. and an approximate 95% of students post-graduation find employment within six months.

But it wasn't just the Brits at the top — the U.S. took the remaining eight spots to round out the top 10 universities. Other countries in the "best of" conversation include Canada, China, and Switzerland. Check out the 10 best universities (OK, 12, since there were two ties) in the world below, then head over to _Times Higher Education_ to see [the full list](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) — and where your school nets out. You might just find something to inspire you to take action and foster change.

About Harvard University

Basic information and contact details for Harvard University

Dating back to 1636, Harvard University is the oldest university in the US and is regarded as one of the most prestigious in the world.

It was named after its first benefactor, John Harvard, who left his library and half his estate to the institution when he died in 1638.

The private Ivy League institution has connections to more than 45 Nobel laureates, over 30 heads of state and 48 Pulitzer prizewinners. It has more than 323,000 living alumni, including over 271,000 in the US and nearly 52,000 in 201 other countries. Thirteen US presidents have honorary degrees from the institution; the most recent of these was awarded to John F. Kennedy in 1956.

Faculty members who have been awarded a Nobel prize in recent years include chemist Martin Karplus and economist Alvin Roth, while notable alumni who were given the honour include former US vice-president Al Gore, who won the Peace Prize in 2007, and poet Seamus Heaney, who was a professor at Harvard from 1981 to 1997.

Situated in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Harvard’s 5,000-acre campus houses 12 degree-granting schools in addition to the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, two theatres and five museums. It is also home to the largest academic library in the world, with 20.4 million volumes, 180,000 serial titles, an estimated 400 million manuscript items, 10 million photographs, 124 million archived web pages and 5.4 terabytes of born-digital archives and manuscripts.

There are more than 400 student organisations on campus, and Harvard’s medical school is connected to 10 hospitals.

The university receives one of the largest financial endowments of any higher education institution in the world; it created $1.5 billion in the fiscal year ended June 2013 – more than a third of Harvard’s total operating revenue in that year.

Harvard’s official colour is crimson, following a vote in 1910, after two student rowers provided crimson scarves to their teammates so that spectators could differentiate the university’s team during a regatta in 1858.

About Harvard University

Basic information and contact details for Harvard University

Dating back to 1636, Harvard University is the oldest university in the US and is regarded as one of the most prestigious in the world.

It was named after its first benefactor, John Harvard, who left his library and half his estate to the institution when he died in 1638.

The private Ivy League institution has connections to more than 45 Nobel laureates, over 30 heads of state and 48 Pulitzer prizewinners. It has more than 323,000 living alumni, including over 271,000 in the US and nearly 52,000 in 201 other countries. Thirteen US presidents have honorary degrees from the institution; the most recent of these was awarded to John F. Kennedy in 1956.

Faculty members who have been awarded a Nobel prize in recent years include chemist Martin Karplus and economist Alvin Roth, while notable alumni who were given the honour include former US vice-president Al Gore, who won the Peace Prize in 2007, and poet Seamus Heaney, who was a professor at Harvard from 1981 to 1997.

Situated in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Harvard’s 5,000-acre campus houses 12 degree-granting schools in addition to the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study, two theatres and five museums. It is also home to the largest academic library in the world, with 20.4 million volumes, 180,000 serial titles, an estimated 400 million manuscript items, 10 million photographs, 124 million archived web pages and 5.4 terabytes of born-digital archives and manuscripts.

There are more than 400 student organisations on campus, and Harvard’s medical school is connected to 10 hospitals.

The university receives one of the largest financial endowments of any higher education institution in the world; it created $1.5 billion in the fiscal year ended June 2013 – more than a third of Harvard’s total operating revenue in that year.

Harvard’s official colour is crimson, following a vote in 1910, after two student rowers provided crimson scarves to their teammates so that spectators could differentiate the university’s team during a regatta in 1858.

THE World Reputation Rankings 2018: methodology explained
Our Academic Reputation Survey underpins these rankings, ensuring that they’re built on the considered judgement of a representative sample of global experts
Published on May 30, 2018
Last updated March 21, 2022
Share on bluesky

Browse the full Times Higher Education World Reputation Rankings 2018 results

The Times Higher Education World Reputation Rankings are created using the world’s largest invitation-only academic opinion survey – a unique piece of research.

The Academic Reputation Survey, available in 15 languages, uses United Nations data as a guide to ensure that the response coverage is as representative of world scholarship as possible. It is also evenly spread across academic disciplines.

The questionnaire, which is administered on behalf of THE by Elsevier, targets only experienced, published scholars, who offer their views on excellence in research and teaching within their disciplines and at institutions with which they are familiar.

The 2018 rankings are based on a survey carried out between January 2018 and March 2018, which received a total of 10,162 responses from 138 countries.

Field work

We have worked hard to ensure a balanced spread of responses across the disciplines. The best represented subject was engineering and technology (accounting for 18.1 per cent of responses), followed by physical sciences (15.6 per cent). Also well represented were clinical and health (13.2 per cent), life sciences (12.8 per cent) and computer science (10.4 per cent). The rest of the responses came from business and economics (9 per cent), social sciences (7.6 per cent), arts and humanities (7.5 per cent), education (2.5 per cent), psychology (2.3 per cent) and law (1 per cent).

However, to better reflect the opinion of scholars from a wide range of disciplines and to make direct comparisons with last year’s ranking, THE’s data team weighted the responses based on the share of votes in each subject from last year’s survey. These were as follows: physical sciences (14.6 per cent), clinical and health (14.5 per cent), life sciences (13.3 per cent), business and economics (13.1 per cent), engineering (12.7 per cent), arts and humanities (12.5 per cent), social sciences (8.9 per cent), computer science (4.2 per cent), education (2.6 per cent), psychology (2.7 per cent), law (0.9 per cent).

ADVERTISEMENT

We have also maintained a fair distribution of survey responses across the regions. A total of 22 per cent of responses hail from North America. The rest of the responses break down as follows: the Asia Pacific region accounted for 32 per cent, western Europe for 26 per cent, eastern Europe for 11 per cent, Latin America for 5 per cent, the Middle East (2 per cent) and Africa (2 per cent).

Where countries were over- or under-represented, THE’s data team weighted the responses to more closely reflect the actual geographical distribution of scholars, based on UN data.

In the survey, scholars are questioned at the level of their specific subject discipline. They are not asked to create a ranking themselves or to list a large range of institutions; they only name at most 15 universities that they believe are the best in each category (research and teaching), based on their own experience.

The survey data will be used alongside 11 objective indicators to help create the THE World University Rankings 2019, which will be unveiled in September 2018.

The reputation table ranks institutions according to an overall measure of their esteem that combines data on their reputation for research and teaching.

The two scores are combined at a ratio of 2:1, giving more weight to research because our expert advisers have suggested that there is greater confidence in respondents’ ability to make accurate judgements about research quality.

The scores are based on the number of times that an institution is cited by respondents as being the best in their field. The number one institution, Harvard University, was the one selected most often. The scores for all other institutions in the table are expressed as a percentage of Harvard’s, which is set at 100.

For example, the University of Oxford received 71.2 per cent of the number of nominations that Harvard gained, giving it a score of 71.2 against Harvard’s 100. This scoring system, which differs from that used in the THE World University Rankings, is intended to give a clearer and more meaningful perspective on the reputation data in isolation.

ADVERTISEMENT

The top 100 universities by reputation are listed, but THE has decided to rank only the top 50 because the differentials between institutions after that point become narrow. The institutions that make up the second half of the table are listed in groups of 10, in alphabetical order, although the number in each group may vary owing to some institutions at the thresholds having the same scores.

THE World Reputation Rankings 2018: methodology explained
Our Academic Reputation Survey underpins these rankings, ensuring that they’re built on the considered judgement of a representative sample of global experts
Published on May 30, 2018
Last updated March 21, 2022
Share on bluesky
Share on linkedin

Browse the full Times Higher Education World Reputation Rankings 2018 results

The Times Higher Education World Reputation Rankings are created using the world’s largest invitation-only academic opinion survey – a unique piece of research.

The Academic Reputation Survey, available in 15 languages, uses United Nations data as a guide to ensure that the response coverage is as representative of world scholarship as possible. It is also evenly spread across academic disciplines.

The questionnaire, which is administered on behalf of THE by Elsevier, targets only experienced, published scholars, who offer their views on excellence in research and teaching within their disciplines and at institutions with which they are familiar.

The 2018 rankings are based on a survey carried out between January 2018 and March 2018, which received a total of 10,162 responses from 138 countries.

Field work

We have worked hard to ensure a balanced spread of responses across the disciplines. The best represented subject was engineering and technology (accounting for 18.1 per cent of responses), followed by physical sciences (15.6 per cent). Also well represented were clinical and health (13.2 per cent), life sciences (12.8 per cent) and computer science (10.4 per cent). The rest of the responses came from business and economics (9 per cent), social sciences (7.6 per cent), arts and humanities (7.5 per cent), education (2.5 per cent), psychology (2.3 per cent) and law (1 per cent).

However, to better reflect the opinion of scholars from a wide range of disciplines and to make direct comparisons with last year’s ranking, THE’s data team weighted the responses based on the share of votes in each subject from last year’s survey. These were as follows: physical sciences (14.6 per cent), clinical and health (14.5 per cent), life sciences (13.3 per cent), business and economics (13.1 per cent), engineering (12.7 per cent), arts and humanities (12.5 per cent), social sciences (8.9 per cent), computer science (4.2 per cent), education (2.6 per cent), psychology (2.7 per cent), law (0.9 per cent).

ADVERTISEMENT

We have also maintained a fair distribution of survey responses across the regions. A total of 22 per cent of responses hail from North America. The rest of the responses break down as follows: the Asia Pacific region accounted for 32 per cent, western Europe for 26 per cent, eastern Europe for 11 per cent, Latin America for 5 per cent, the Middle East (2 per cent) and Africa (2 per cent).

Where countries were over- or under-represented, THE’s data team weighted the responses to more closely reflect the actual geographical distribution of scholars, based on UN data.

In the survey, scholars are questioned at the level of their specific subject discipline. They are not asked to create a ranking themselves or to list a large range of institutions; they only name at most 15 universities that they believe are the best in each category (research and teaching), based on their own experience.

The survey data will be used alongside 11 objective indicators to help create the THE World University Rankings 2019, which will be unveiled in September 2018.

The reputation table ranks institutions according to an overall measure of their esteem that combines data on their reputation for research and teaching.

The two scores are combined at a ratio of 2:1, giving more weight to research because our expert advisers have suggested that there is greater confidence in respondents’ ability to make accurate judgements about research quality.

The scores are based on the number of times that an institution is cited by respondents as being the best in their field. The number one institution, Harvard University, was the one selected most often. The scores for all other institutions in the table are expressed as a percentage of Harvard’s, which is set at 100.

For example, the University of Oxford received 71.2 per cent of the number of nominations that Harvard gained, giving it a score of 71.2 against Harvard’s 100. This scoring system, which differs from that used in the THE World University Rankings, is intended to give a clearer and more meaningful perspective on the reputation data in isolation.

ADVERTISEMENT

The top 100 universities by reputation are listed, but THE has decided to rank only the top 50 because the differentials between institutions after that point become narrow. The institutions that make up the second half of the table are listed in groups of 10, in alphabetical order, although the number in each group may vary owing to some institutions at the thresholds having the same scores.

Prospective students who wish to study in the most international environments in the world should apply to universities in Switzerland, Hong Kong, the UAE or the UK.

Universities, by their nature, are global institutions. Typically, they are home to communities of students and scholars from all over the world, and they tackle some of the globe’s most pressing problems through research.

This table – compiled using the international student score, international staff score, international co-authorship score and international reputation metrics collected for the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026 – shows that the above four regions are home to some of the most international universities in the world.

These institutions all have a high proportion of international students and staff, collaborate on research with scholars from across the world, and have a strong global reputation to match. Read the full methodology at the bottom of the page.

Research suggests that diverse communities of students improve the teaching and learning experience, while opportunities for students to spend time abroad better prepare them to become global citizens.

Top five most international universities in the world
1. City University of Hong Kong

City University of Hong Kong is a public research university in Kowloon, Hong Kong. It was founded in 1984 as the City Polytechnic of Hong Kong, and it became a fully accredited university in 1994.

There are 11 colleges and schools: biomedicine, business, computing, engineering, liberal arts and social sciences, science, veterinary medicine and life sciences, creative media, data science, energy and environment, law, and graduate studies.

The university set up the Distinguished Visiting Professor Scheme in 2023. The scheme invites over 50 internationally renowned scholars to conduct interdisciplinary scientific and academic research with CityUHK faculty and students.

The student body is drawn from nearly 100 countries/regions and its faculty come from more than 40 countries or regions.

2. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology is regarded as one of the fastest-growing universities in the world.

More than a third of the student body is considered international with at least 60 nationalities represented. About 80 per cent of the faculty come from overseas.

More than 45 per cent of students undertake an overseas exchange and all four academic schools have their own exchange programmes. Some 70 per cent of students participate in internships overseas. 

3. University of Hong Kong

The University of Hong Kong has embarked on a mission to become “Asia’s Global University”, which includes the goal of 50 per cent of its undergraduates having two opportunities to study outside Hong Kong during their degree.

Overall, Hong Kong’s leading university has more than 20,000 students, with almost 8,000 from abroad.

Teaching at the institution is in English and education has an international focus, with the aim of preparing students to become global citizens who could be successful anywhere in the world.

Hong Kong itself is also known as one of the most global cities in the world, acting as a gateway between East and West.

4. Imperial College London

Imperial College London focuses teaching and learning around science, engineering, medicine and business.

Imperial College London is consistently ranked among the best universities in the world for science, technology, engineering, medicine and business.

More than 60 per cent of students are international students coming from over 140 countries.

Clubs and support services for international students at Imperial College include the International Family Network and the International Students House. 

5. Abu Dhabi University

Abu Dhabi University was established in 2003 and enrols about 8,000 students.

The university is home to students from more than 100 nations.

There are many opportunities for international students to become part of the community, such as through clubs and sports teams, the student council, and volunteering and community outreach initiatives.

The university also publishes an undergraduate and postgraduate handbook to help students learn about life on campus and the facilities and services available to them.

Methodology

The data in Times Higher Education’s ranking of the World’s Most International Universities 2026 is drawn mainly from the “international outlook” pillar of the THE World University Rankings 2026. This takes into account a university’s proportion of international students, international staff and journal publications with at least one international co-author. Each of these elements is given equal weighting in calculating the score for this pillar.

The table adds a fourth component, which makes up 25 per cent of the total score: a university’s international reputation. This is a measure of the proportion of votes from outside the home country that the institution achieved in THE’s annual invitation-only Academic Reputation Survey, which asks leading scholars to name the world’s best universities for teaching and research in their field.

Only institutions that received at least 400 votes in the survey were eligible for inclusion. Universities must also receive at least 200 or at least 10 per cent of available domestic votes to be ranked. Once universities are included in the international list, they are excluded only if they do not meet the vote thresholds for two years in a row.

Metrics and weightings:

• 25 per cent: proportion of international staff

• 25 per cent: proportion of international students

• 25 per cent: international co-authorship

• 25 per cent: international reputation.

Prospective students who wish to study in the most international environments in the world should apply to universities in Switzerland, Hong Kong, the UAE or the UK.

Universities, by their nature, are global institutions. Typically, they are home to communities of students and scholars from all over the world, and they tackle some of the globe’s most pressing problems through research.

This table – compiled using the international student score, international staff score, international co-authorship score and international reputation metrics collected for the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026 – shows that the above four regions are home to some of the most international universities in the world.

These institutions all have a high proportion of international students and staff, collaborate on research with scholars from across the world, and have a strong global reputation to match. Read the full methodology at the bottom of the page.

Research suggests that diverse communities of students improve the teaching and learning experience, while opportunities for students to spend time abroad better prepare them to become global citizens.

Top five most international universities in the world
1. City University of Hong Kong

City University of Hong Kong is a public research university in Kowloon, Hong Kong. It was founded in 1984 as the City Polytechnic of Hong Kong, and it became a fully accredited university in 1994.

There are 11 colleges and schools: biomedicine, business, computing, engineering, liberal arts and social sciences, science, veterinary medicine and life sciences, creative media, data science, energy and environment, law, and graduate studies.

The university set up the Distinguished Visiting Professor Scheme in 2023. The scheme invites over 50 internationally renowned scholars to conduct interdisciplinary scientific and academic research with CityUHK faculty and students.

The student body is drawn from nearly 100 countries/regions and its faculty come from more than 40 countries or regions.

2. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology is regarded as one of the fastest-growing universities in the world.

More than a third of the student body is considered international with at least 60 nationalities represented. About 80 per cent of the faculty come from overseas.

More than 45 per cent of students undertake an overseas exchange and all four academic schools have their own exchange programmes. Some 70 per cent of students participate in internships overseas. 

3. University of Hong Kong

The University of Hong Kong has embarked on a mission to become “Asia’s Global University”, which includes the goal of 50 per cent of its undergraduates having two opportunities to study outside Hong Kong during their degree.

Overall, Hong Kong’s leading university has more than 20,000 students, with almost 8,000 from abroad.

Teaching at the institution is in English and education has an international focus, with the aim of preparing students to become global citizens who could be successful anywhere in the world.

Hong Kong itself is also known as one of the most global cities in the world, acting as a gateway between East and West.

4. Imperial College London

Imperial College London focuses teaching and learning around science, engineering, medicine and business.

Imperial College London is consistently ranked among the best universities in the world for science, technology, engineering, medicine and business.

More than 60 per cent of students are international students coming from over 140 countries.

Clubs and support services for international students at Imperial College include the International Family Network and the International Students House. 

5. Abu Dhabi University

Abu Dhabi University was established in 2003 and enrols about 8,000 students.

The university is home to students from more than 100 nations.

There are many opportunities for international students to become part of the community, such as through clubs and sports teams, the student council, and volunteering and community outreach initiatives.

The university also publishes an undergraduate and postgraduate handbook to help students learn about life on campus and the facilities and services available to them.

Further analysis of the results can be found here

Methodology

The data in Times Higher Education’s ranking of the World’s Most International Universities 2026 is drawn mainly from the “international outlook” pillar of the THE World University Rankings 2026. This takes into account a university’s proportion of international students, international staff and journal publications with at least one international co-author. Each of these elements is given equal weighting in calculating the score for this pillar.

The table adds a fourth component, which makes up 25 per cent of the total score: a university’s international reputation. This is a measure of the proportion of votes from outside the home country that the institution achieved in THE’s annual invitation-only Academic Reputation Survey, which asks leading scholars to name the world’s best universities for teaching and research in their field.

Only institutions that received at least 400 votes in the survey were eligible for inclusion. Universities must also receive at least 200 or at least 10 per cent of available domestic votes to be ranked. Once universities are included in the international list, they are excluded only if they do not meet the vote thresholds for two years in a row.

Metrics and weightings:

• 25 per cent: proportion of international staff

• 25 per cent: proportion of international students

• 25 per cent: international co-authorship

• 25 per cent: international reputation.

Editor’s note: As part of our THE statement on Ukraine published on 2 March 2022, Russian universities have been given less prominence in our rankings. Russian universities that met the criteria for this ranking are not displayed in the table above.

# World University Rankings by Subject 2018: Physical Sciences

You are currently viewing a previous year's ranking.

Explore the latest ranking:[Physical Sciences](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2026/subject-ranking/physical-sciences)

The 2018 _Times Higher Education_ World University Rankings’ table for physical sciences subjects employs the same rigorous and balanced range of 13 performance indicators used in the overall World University Rankings, but the methodology has been recalibrated to suit the individual fields.

It highlights the universities that are leading across mathematics, statistics, physics, astronomy, chemistry, geology and environmental sciences subjects.

[**View the World University Rankings 2018 by subject: physical sciences methodology**](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/subject-ranking-2018-physical-sciences-methodology)

[Princeton University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/princeton-university) tops the table for the first time since 2015. Princeton’s industry income score increased dramatically this year, while its teaching environment also improved. Overall the US dominates the table, claiming 115 places.

# University of Oxford Tops Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2018

Check out the list.

By [Rachel Jacoby Zoldan](https://www.teenvogue.com/contributor/rachel-jacoby-zoldan)

September 5, 2017

It seems that every day there's a new college ranking system, whether it be the school with the best [value](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/forbes-ranks-best-value-colleges) — or the [most parties](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/princeton-review-2018-college-rankings). But the best universities in the world have been compiled for 2018 in one neat list from the [_Times Higher Education_](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) and its corresponding, in-depth [data report](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2018/world-ranking#!/page/0/length/25/locations/CA/sort_by/rank/sort_order/asc/cols/stats). And for the first time _ever_, the U.K. snagged the top two spots, with Oxford University coming in at number one and Cambridge University just behind it at number two.

To definitively rank the universities, of which they culled data from thousands of in over 77 countries, the _Times Higher Education_[looked at five primary factors](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/methodology-world-university-rankings-2018) within each school: "research, teaching, research influence, industry income, and international outlook." Translation: They looked at each college or university's learning environment, the overall efficacy and success of its research, and generally how well knowledge flows on campus. Oxford University was the overall best for the second year in a row; it's the oldest university in the U.K. and an approximate 95% of students post-graduation find employment within six months.

But it wasn't just the Brits at the top — the U.S. took the remaining eight spots to round out the top 10 universities. Other countries in the "best of" conversation include Canada, China, and Switzerland. Check out the 10 best universities (OK, 12, since there were two ties) in the world below, then head over to _Times Higher Education_ to see [the full list](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/student/best-universities/best-universities-world#survey-answer) — and where your school nets out. You might just find something to inspire you to take action and foster change.
